blocks.text: On ==10 September 1964==, a baby was born in Hangzhou, a lake city about 100 miles southwest of Shanghai. His parents named him Yun, which means “cloud”. His family name, Ma, is the same as the Chinese word for horse. Nobody in that house was thinking about companies, because in China at that moment there were almost none left to think about.

He was the middle child of three, in what the University of Hong Kong later called a very modest household. Today his birthday is also China's Teachers' Day. It is a small coincidence, but it fits: teaching is the only job he ever trained for.
Born on Teachers' Day. Teaching is the only job he trained for.

For example: by the time Ma was born, about 90 per cent of China's industrial production had been taken over by the state. The future king of private trade arrived in a country where private trade had nearly been wiped out.
Two ordinary jobs, one shared love

His mother, Cui Wencai, worked on a factory line, reported in one profile as a garment factory. His father, Ma Laifa, was a photographer at a photo agency and ran a local drama association on the side. These were low-level jobs, and a 2008 profile says the family's bad class background kept them there.

What joined the two of them was pingtan, a folk art of sung ballads and comic routines, punctuated by wooden clappers. Some reports call his parents professional pingtan performers. His biographer Duncan Clark describes it as a shared passion alongside their day jobs. Either way, the house was full of it.
As a kid, in the evenings, I would listen to people talking about stories.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, to Worth magazine, 2008

blocks.text: Both Clark and the Associated Press suggest this may be where his gift came from. A pingtan performer has a voice, a pair of clappers and a room of people who can walk out. __The first business skill Ma ever watched up close was not accounting. It was holding a room.__
Before maths, before English: he learned how a storyteller keeps a crowd.
The wrong kind of family

When he was two, Mao launched the Cultural Revolution. Red Guards attacked the “Four Olds”, meaning old customs, culture, habits and ideas. In Hangzhou they badly damaged the tomb of the Song dynasty general Yue Fei. Pingtan was banned as a target of the campaign, and the people who practised it were denounced.

The Ma family had a second problem. Jack's grandfather had been a local official under the Nationalists, the side that lost the civil war. In Mao's China that label followed a family around. Classmates taunted the boy for it, although the family was never broken up, as many others were.

photo.caption: West Lake, Hangzhou, photographed in 1987. This lake was the backdrop of Jack Ma's whole childhood.
photo.author: Nathan Hughes Hamilton from Sacramento, California, USA

blocks.text: Thirteen stitches

He was tiny, and classmates teased him for it. He fought anyway. Chinese profiles describe him as the student who got into more fights than anyone else at school, and say he fought for friends, not for himself. He imagined himself as a wandering hero out of a martial arts novel.

In fourth grade, one fight to protect someone else left him so badly cut that the bone showed. The hospital had no anaesthetic, so they stitched him without it. Over those years the stitches added up to ==13==, along with punishments at school.
It really hurt, but I didn't shed a single tear.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, on the fourth-grade fight, to IT Times, 2007 (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: Fighting for friends as a kid. Eighteen people later followed him into a flat.

Home was not always calm either. Chinese profiles describe a hot-tempered father who disciplined him physically. Yet that same anger gave Jack his first reason to care about English. When he was young, he picked up a few words from other children, and he found a new way to answer back.
My dad scolded me, so I answered back in English. He couldn't understand, which felt great, so I kept learning, and the more I learned the more I liked it.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, as reported by p5w.net, 2015 (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: Crickets, novels and a pocket radio

He had the obsessions of a boy with no money. A friend from those years remembers him as passionate about cricket fighting, with an expert ear for the sounds made by different kinds of the insect. He went with his grandmother to Buddhist temples to burn incense. He hung around teahouses where locals played Chinese chess and cards and told tall tales.

Above all he read the martial arts novels of Jin Yong, the pen name of Louis Cha. His favourite character was Feng Qingyang, an unpredictable old swordmaster who teaches a younger hero. Decades later, “Feng Qingyang” was Ma's own nickname inside Alibaba, and he encouraged staff to take names from the same novels.
His favourite childhood novels ended up naming the staff of Alibaba.

Then came the radio. In February 1972, when he was seven, President Nixon visited Hangzhou during his historic China trip. At around 12, Ma bought a pocket radio and began listening to English broadcasts every day. Clark says he especially loved readings of Tom Sawyer on shortwave.
I don't know why at 12, 13 years old, at that time I suddenly fell in love with the language, English.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, to Charlie Rose, World Economic Forum, Davos, 2015

blocks.text: Bad at the one thing that counted

School was going badly, and maths was the reason. By his own telling, he failed a key primary school test twice and failed for middle school three times. China's school system sorts children by exam results, so each failure pushed him into a lesser school. He was never in a first-rate school at any stage.
It was changed from primary school to middle school because our graduates of our school, no middle school accept us because we're too bad.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, on the school he ended up in, Davos, 2015

blocks.text: A school invented because nobody would take them. That was his starting line.

So picture him at 12. He is small, poor at maths, marked by his family history and known for his fists. His neighbours and teachers had little hope for him, says one 2007 profile. But he also has three things that do not show up on a report card: a love of stories, loyalty to friends, and a radio speaking a language almost nobody around him knows.

items.text: Ma Yun is born in Hangzhou, the middle of three children.
Aged two. The Cultural Revolution begins, and pingtan and his family's past become dangerous.
Aged seven. Nixon visits Hangzhou, and the city is on its way to welcoming foreigners again.
A fight for a friend ends with stitches and no anaesthetic.
Aged about 12. He buys a pocket radio and falls for English.
Aged 14. China announces its open-door policy. Only 728 foreign tourists visited Hangzhou that year.

blocks.title: Your early weakness does not have to be your whole story
blocks.text: Ma was bad at the thing school measured and good at things it did not. His mistake was treating school as an enemy and letting maths collapse, and it cost him years. What he got right was finding the one skill he loved and feeding it every day.

At 13 he had collected so many demerits for fighting that he was forced to move to Hangzhou No. 8 Middle School. He then needed two attempts to reach even an ordinary high school, scoring 31 in maths on one of them. English class was no great help either. One Chinese profile says it was taught by a Chinese-language teacher who studied the lesson for two hours in the morning and taught it in the afternoon.
So he taught himself. There were no English books around and nowhere to take classes. He went to where the English was.
Five o'clock at the Hangzhou Hotel

Look at these two numbers. In ==1978==, only ==728== foreign tourists visited Hangzhou. The next year, after Deng Xiaoping opened the country, more than ==40,000== came. The place to find them was the Hangzhou Hotel by West Lake, where Nixon's party had stayed and which is now a Shangri-La. One visitor remembers it as the only hotel in the city open to Westerners at the time.

Ma began waking before dawn and riding his bicycle for 40 minutes to its front door. He would stand there reading English, waiting for foreigners to come out. Then he made them an offer that was hard to refuse: a free guided tour of the lake, in exchange for talking to him. He kept this up in rain and snow, for eight or nine years depending on which interview you read.
I'd give them a free tour of West Lake, and they taught me English. For nine years!
blocks.who: Jack Ma, quoted in Duncan Clark's Alibaba

blocks.text: For example: nine years of mornings is roughly 3,000 trips to that hotel, if you take “every morning” at his word. Years later he reckoned he had shown round at least 2,000 foreign visitors. That is 2,000 conversations in a foreign language, with strangers he first had to win over.
No fees, no teacher. Just a bicycle and the nerve to say hello.

Here is the part most people miss. The tourists were not only fixing his grammar. They told him things about the world that did not match what he heard at school. __The real product of those mornings was not English. It was a second way of seeing.__
I think that was the nine years these western tourists opened my mind.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, Davos, 2015

blocks.text: He also got his name there. An American tourist became his pen friend and found “Ma Yun” hard to say, so she asked if he had an English name. He said no, and asked her to give him one. By his account, she answered: “My father's called Jack, my husband's called Jack, what do you think about Jack?”

photo.caption: The Broken Bridge on West Lake, in a modern photo. The lake was the classroom where a teenage Ma traded free tours for English.
photo.author: Yinweichen

blocks.text: The boy flicking matches

In July 1980, an Australian family reached Hangzhou on a tour with the Australia-China Friendship Society. The father, Ken Morley, was a Newcastle electrical engineer, a union organiser and a Communist who wanted to show his children the socialist world. On a free evening, his son David slipped across the road from the hotel to the park to flick matches. Ma was 15.
I had gone down to the West Lake in Hangzhou to flick matches and this boy came up to me who could speak English.
blocks.who: David Morley, to the Australian Financial Review, 2016

blocks.text: They met again and played Frisbee in the park, using shoes to mark out the field. David told Clark they were soon surrounded by hundreds of Chinese spectators, and Ma's father took photographs. Ken Morley's first impression of this eager kid was a “barrow boy”, a street hawker. When the Morleys flew home, Ma kept writing.

For example: Ken Morley told Ma to double-space his letters. That way Ken could write corrections in the gaps and post the original back along with his own reply. It was a private English course by airmail, from a stranger on the other side of the world.
A near-stranger marked his homework by post for years. Find your Ken Morley.

One month later, in August 1980, a 28-year-old American lawyer named Bruce Thelen came out of the same hotel on a one-year trip round the world. A skinny boy offered to show him the city. Thelen spent half a day with him and never forgot it. Thirty-seven years later, at an Alibaba event in Detroit, he held up a sign reminding Ma that he had once been his tour guide.
He was only 16, hovering around the hotel and looking for anyone appearing to speak English.
blocks.who: Bruce Thelen, to CGTN, 2017

blocks.text: Thelen joked that Ma's English was better at 16.
One out of 120
In 1982, the year he turned 18, he sat the gaokao, the national university entrance exam. He had put Peking University on his form. His maths score came back: ==1 out of 120==. That is not a typo.

He went looking for work with his cousin. Both applied to wait tables at a hotel. The cousin got the job; Ma was told he was too short and too thin. In those same lost years, one profile says, the army and a police school also turned him down.

So the boy who talked to foreigners at dawn did what work he could find, as a secretary and a porter. Through his father's connections he got a job pedalling a three-wheeled cart, delivering bundles of magazines for publishers to the train station. One biography-based account gives his wage as ==30.5 yuan a month==.
Some of his first wages came from pedalling magazines. Nothing clever about it.
The novel at the train station

Then, on a work errand, he bought a book at the railway station in Yiwu. It was Life, a new novel by the Shaanxi writer Lu Yao, about a talented village youth named Gao Jialin who struggles to escape poverty. Ma has said he came away thinking that this man failed and tried again, while he himself had failed and gone off to pedal a cart.
I thought: he worked that hard, so I should make an effort too.
blocks.who: Jack Ma on Lu Yao's novel Life (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: In 1983 he sat the exam again. Maths rose to ==19 out of 120==, but his total fell, and he failed. His parents tried to talk him out of trying again. One account says only his father still backed him and found him a maths tutor, while other reports simply say the family was against it. A teacher told him that if he ever passed, the teacher would write their own name backwards.

He kept working. He applied for job after job, and every Sunday he rose early and travelled more than an hour to the Zhejiang University library. There he memorised the maths formulas he had never understood. One account stresses that this third try was his own decision, taken against nearly everyone's advice.

items.label: Maths score, third attempt, 1984 (79 in some reports)
How far his total still fell short of the degree line

blocks.text: In 1984, at 19, he passed on the third try, though not by much. He was still five points below the line for a four-year degree. He should have been sent to a shorter course. But Hangzhou Teachers College had not filled its places for the English degree, and it had a few left for male students. So he slid in through the side door, on the strength of his one great subject.
I flunked my exam for university two times before I was accepted by what was considered my city's worst university.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, to Inc. magazine, 2008

blocks.text: Look at what actually saved him. It was not a maths miracle. It was those thousands of mornings at the hotel door, which had made his English strong enough to win a spare seat. __The skill nobody had asked him to build opened the door that the skill everyone demanded had shut.__

photo.caption: A street scene in Shanghai, about 100 miles from Hangzhou, in 1982, the year Ma failed his first university entrance exam.
photo.author: H. Grobe

blocks.title: Practise the thing nobody is making you practise
blocks.text: No one assigned Ma those mornings at the hotel. They paid nothing, and they would not raise his maths score. They gave him English, a view of the outside world and his first friendships abroad. When you are 16 and failing at the official game, a stubborn side skill can become your way in.
The worst college, the best years

With maths gone from his life, the failing student became a star. He stayed in the top five of his department. In his second year he was elected president of the student union, and he launched a campus singing contest. He then served two terms as president of the Hangzhou Students Federation.

He ran that union like a tiny startup. There was no money, so he borrowed. One profile says that for one event he went to six nearby colleges to borrow equipment, carrying it himself by bicycle, because pedalling was the one thing his cart job had made him great at. A former teacher remembers asking students to come up and share their experience, and the whole class refusing except for one. That one was Ma, and the teacher later gave him two class hours to talk about his trip to Australia.
Student union work is real training. He got things done with no money.

He also met Zhang Ying there, a fellow student who went by Cathy in English. She would later be one of his first employees. Her own verdict, given in an interview, is one of the best lines in this book: “Ma Yun is not a handsome man, but I fell for him because he can do a lot of things handsome men cannot do.”
Twenty-nine days in New Lambton

In 1985 Ken Morley invited him to Australia. Getting there was its own battle: his visa application was rejected ==seven times==. In July he finally landed, 20 years old and leaving China for the first time, and went to stay in the Newcastle suburb of New Lambton.
Before I left China, I was educated that China was the richest, happiest country in the world. So when I arrived in Australia, I thought, Oh, my God, everything is different from what I was told.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, to Inc. magazine, 2008

blocks.text: The Morleys did ordinary things with him, like a visit to Sydney's Taronga Zoo. He showed a local tai chi group his monkey-style and drunken-style kung fu in a suburban hall. And Ken Morley argued with him. As Ma told it in Newcastle in 2017: “He'd say, Jack, you're bullshit …. but he always supported me”.
When I went back to China I became a different Jack Ma, the Jack Ma standing in front of you.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, Newcastle, Australia, 2017

photo.caption: Nobbys Beach, Newcastle, New South Wales, in a recent photo. Ma spent 29 days in this city in 1985 and later called it his second hometown.
photo.author: Dicklyon

blocks.text: The help did not stop with letters. College tuition was free, but the live-in fees were a strain, so Morley sent a cheque every six months. One report totals this at about 200 Australian dollars over two years. Later the Morleys gave Ma and Cathy ==A$22,000== towards their first home. Ken visited most years to help at the college where Ma taught.

Ken Morley died in 2004, after Ma had flown out to see him one last time. In 2017, Ma returned to Newcastle and gave the university ==US$20 million== for scholarships in the Morley name. It was the largest gift in its history. __Ma's Communist friend, as his biographer points out, had helped create one of the great capitalists of the age.__

items.label: Visa rejections before his first trip abroad
His stay in Newcastle in 1985, by his 2017 telling
Roughly what Morley sent during college, in small cheques
What Ma gave back to Morley's home town

blocks.text: Very important: remember who helped when you had nothing. He did.
Ninety yuan a month

In 1988, Ma graduated. By his account he was the only one of 500 students assigned to teach at a university rather than a school. The vice-president in charge of placements, Huang Shumeng, recommended him to a nearby engineering college that badly needed English teachers. Huang's only worry was that this restless boy would not stay. On leaving day, he walked him to the college gate himself.
You're the first graduate I've sent to teach at a university. You must stay at least five years.
blocks.who: Huang Shumeng to Ma Yun, 1988 (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: So at 23 he joined the Hangzhou Institute of Electronic Engineering, on a monthly wage of ==90 yuan==, later 120. He told Inc. that his pay was like $12 to $15 a month. Many of the new teachers there came from famous universities such as Tsinghua and Peking. In his dormitory, Building 6, Room 104, his shelves held complete sets of Jin Yong and Liang Yusheng, and a long punching bag hung from the ceiling.

Students were invited back to box and to argue about novels. A colleague says they saw him less as a teacher than as a big brother. In class he came alive. His student Jiang Fang remembers him lighting up the room, sitting down on the lectern mid-story and running on until the bell. One student recalls that he never prepared a lesson, yet everyone's interest in English rose.

He was tough as well as fun. Jiang Fang says he made first-years memorise the first 100 passages of a textbook, and that he marked harder than anyone. When her group sat the national English test in their first year, he told them they would pass. Only one student in two classes failed. Later, his students Jiang Fang, Han Min and Dai Shan would give up safe graduate careers to follow him.
I teach really well, truly great! I feel my teaching may have reached perfection!
blocks.who: Jack Ma, in an old classroom video (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: Confidence first, results later. Do you see where the Alibaba speeches come from?

Then the outside world started calling. One offer from Shenzhen paid 1,200 yuan a month. Another, from Hainan, paid 3,600. He was tempted. He has said he stayed because he had given Huang his word, and he went on to stay well past the five years he had promised.

For example: the Hainan offer was 30 times his salary of 120 yuan. He turned it down for a promise he had made to an old college official at a gate. “A promise is a promise. If I'm not going, I'm not going,” is how he put it in a later speech (translated from Chinese).

At night he kept moving. He taught English at the Hangzhou YMCA. The students, from school pupils to factory workers, loved him because he skipped the grammar and just talked. When the Sunday “English corner” in a park by West Lake was not enough, he launched his own on Wednesday nights. He had worked out that people are less embarrassed to speak bad English in the dark.
Wednesday nights, in the dark, so nobody felt shy. That's product thinking.
The famous KFC story, checked

Every retelling of his life includes the line: when KFC came to his city, 24 people applied, 23 were hired, and he alone was refused. He also tells of the police taking four of five applicants, and of 30 job rejections and 10 letters to Harvard. Some versions, including his biography, place the KFC story right after his exams, in his teens. __The dates say otherwise.__

KFC opened its first China restaurant in Beijing only in ==1987==, and its first in Zhejiang province opened in Hangzhou in ==1993==. So the KFC rejection cannot have happened when he was a teenager. It fits what he told Inc. in 2008. Around 1992, as business opened up, he applied for many jobs while still a teacher, and he was turned down as secretary to the general manager of a KFC.
Even famous stories need checking. We checked this one.
Hope, and the sack of flashlights

In ==January 1994==, at 29, he started his first company on the side. It was a translation agency called Hope, or Haibo in Chinese. He had noticed two things: Hangzhou's trading firms needed translators, and retired teachers were sitting at home with small pensions. There were five staff. It looks like a small idea, but note the shape of it: connect people who need something with people who have it.

It nearly died at once. In the first month it earned 700 yuan and the rent was 2,000. Partners started to waver, and some left. So Ma slung a big sack over his shoulder and went to Yiwu and Guangzhou, buying small goods to resell. For a while, Hangzhou's first professional translation agency was kept alive by flowers, books, clothes, socks and flashlights. The journalist Liu Ren, who interviewed Ma in 2002, adds that he also spent a year selling medicine, to everyone from big hospitals to village doctors.
For example: that first month's loss was 1,300 yuan, which was nearly 11 months of his teaching salary at 120 yuan. He did not close the shop or hunt for investors. He went to the wholesale market.

photo.caption: A shopping mall in Yiwu in 2009. In 1994 Ma came to Yiwu with a sack to buy small goods that would pay his agency's rent.
photo.author: Cherubby

blocks.text: If the business can't pay rent, sell flashlights until it can.
Malibu, a gun and a slot machine

By 1995 word had got around about his English. That is why he was asked to help with a highway project near Hangzhou, where an American investor's money had not appeared after a year of talks. Both sides decided the problem was poor translation, so they brought in Ma. The investor then blamed his board in Hong Kong, and after that the money being held in America, so Ma went to both. It was his first time in the United States.

What follows is Ma's own story, and he has told it in different ways. He says the American locked him up at a house in Malibu and tried to make him part of a scheme. He has never named the man. He has said he talked his way out by promising to start an internet business with him, though he barely knew what the internet was.
At one point, he started playing with his handgun. It was obviously meant as a threat.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, as quoted in Helen H. Wang's The Chinese Dream, excerpted in Forbes

blocks.text: The ending is even stranger. By his telling, he was taken to Las Vegas, where he put a coin in a slot machine and won ==$600==. He walked out without his suitcase and bought a ticket to Seattle. His personal assistant has written that Ma prefers to forget it, and when a Newsweek reporter later asked for details, he declined.
It was really like a classic American-style Hollywood film.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, to the authors of the 2009 book Alibaba

blocks.text: B-E-E-R

Why Seattle? Because of Bill Aho, an American who taught English with him in Hangzhou. Aho had told him about something called the internet, though Ma said Aho could not really explain it either. In Seattle, Ma stayed with Aho's relatives, Dave and Dolores Selig. As he was shown round rich neighbourhoods, he pointed at big houses and said he was going to buy them. They laughed. In Aho's words: “At that time, he didn't have a nickel.”

Then Aho's son-in-law, Stuart Trusty, took him into his internet consultancy in a downtown office tower: two small rooms, by one account, with five young people typing at screens. Ma, who had never touched a keyboard, was scared to touch the computer because he did not think he could afford to pay if he broke it. Then he typed the first word he could think of.
I found American beer, Germany beer, and no Chinese beer. So I was curious. I searched 'China,' and all search engines said no China, no data.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, in the documentary Crocodile in the Yangtze

blocks.text: His new friends put up a very plain page for the Hope agency, with its prices and contact details. It went up in the morning, and Ma went out to see the city. By that same day there were emails waiting: five in most accounts, from places such as America and Japan. One of them said this was the first Chinese company the writer had seen online. A translator with no technical skills had just found a gap the size of a country.

It was my first trip to the States, the first time in my life I touched a keyboard and computers, the first time in my life I connected to the Internet, and the first time I decided to leave as a teacher and start a company.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, quoted in Duncan Clark's Alibaba

blocks.text: Thirty years old and had never touched a keyboard. You are not late.
Twenty-three said no

Back in Hangzhou, one night in March 1995, he invited ==24 friends== to his home. Most were people in foreign trade he had met while teaching evening classes. He told them he was quitting to do the internet, and talked for two hours. They asked five questions, and he could not answer any of them.
They listened in a daze, and I talked in a daze. In the end 23 of them said forget it, and only one said you can try it, and if it fails, run back quickly.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, as quoted by IT Times, 2007 (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: “Open a bar, open a restaurant, run a night school, anything. Just not this,” Liu Ren reports them saying (translated from Chinese). He slept on it, and in the morning he decided to go ahead even if all 24 were against him. He showed his superior at the college, Chen Dingguo, a scrap of paper no bigger than a cigarette box, covered in terms Chen had never heard. Ma's plan was to run a company for ten years and then come back to teach with real experience. He left the college in 1995, having stayed more than six years rather than the five he had promised.

In April 1995 he, Cathy and a computing teacher named He Yibing started China Pages, an online directory of Chinese companies. The starting money was small: about 20,000 yuan, with 7,000 of it his own and the rest from family. He told Inc. it was $2,000, borrowed. __China's public internet was still months away, and he was already selling it.__

The product was comic. To put Hangzhou's Wanghu Hotel online, he had to courier its details to the United States, where the page was built, and then have a printout posted back. If the boss did not believe it, he had to phone America to check. Only then would he pay. Many people assumed Ma was running a scam.
It really was awful to watch. We were just like swindlers.
blocks.who: Jack Ma on selling China Pages, in The Beijing News, 2019 (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: For example: a page of about 3,000 characters and one photo cost a customer 20,000 yuan. Of that, 12,000 went to the American partner who built it. Ma's team kept 8,000, and had to fight for every sale.
Being called a fraud is normal when you sell the future early.
Beijing shuts the door

He took the fight to Beijing. Through a friend he met a driver at the Beijing Youth Daily, handed him an article and 500 yuan, and told him he could keep the money if he got it published anywhere. It reached five outlets, including the front page of a national trade paper. He held a press talk and later lectured officials at the People's Daily, explaining what the internet was.

A fellow Hangzhou native, the state TV producer Fan Xinman, was struck by his energy and filmed a programme called Bookish Ma Yun. It is painful to read about. A thin salesman walks through old alleys full of hope into a government office, and is told to make an appointment and follow the procedure. Accounts say he was driven away as a swindler more than once.

Back home, worse was waiting. In 1996 Hangzhou Telecom launched its own China Pages with a nearly identical name and a vastly bigger budget. Customers drifted over. Ma agreed to merge: his company was valued at 600,000 yuan for 30 per cent, and Telecom put in 1.4 million for 70 per cent.

items.label: Telecom's share vs Ma's in the merged China Pages
The investment, by his account the most money he had ever seen

blocks.text: He soon learned what those numbers meant. “Everything we suggested, they turned us down,” he later said. “It was like an elephant and an ant.” He quit and sold his stake cheaply, by one report for little more than 100,000 yuan. __He lost the company, but his small team came with him, and that turned out to be the part that mattered.__
Read this twice, first-time founders: control matters more than the size of the cheque.
The government job and the tears on the Wall

In 1997 the trade ministry in Beijing invited him to run a new e-commerce unit, and he took his team north. They packed into a rented room of under 20 square metres and lived in shared dormitories. They worked for about 15 months, and according to one report they made a real profit. But the ministry wanted to serve big companies, and he wanted small ones. Equity promised to the team never arrived, one report says.

One small assignment from this job later turned out to be worth billions. In 1997 he was told to take a young visitor named Jerry Yang, the co-founder of Yahoo, on a tour of the Great Wall. He was a tour guide again, just as at 15. Years later, Yahoo paid $1 billion for 40 per cent of Alibaba.
In retrospect, what are the chances.
blocks.who: Jerry Yang on getting Ma as his guide, as reported by Fortune, 2018

blocks.text: One night in 1998 he called the team to his room and laid it out. They could go to Yahoo with his recommendation. They could go to Sina or Sohu. Or they could come back to Hangzhou with him on almost no pay, live within five minutes of the office, and start again. He gave them three days to think. They went out, talked for three minutes, and came back in.

Before leaving Beijing the team climbed the Great Wall together, and on top of it one of them broke down sobbing. There is old film of Ma in the back of a car at night, with red neon sliding past, sounding nothing like the man on stage. “Everything has to start again from the beginning,” he says (translated from Chinese).
If I don't succeed, someone else will.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, filmed in Beijing, as reported by The Beijing News, 2019 (translated from Chinese)

blocks.text: A cold apartment, 21 February 1999

They went home in January 1999. On ==21 February==, in his apartment at Lakeside Gardens in Hangzhou, 18 people gathered: his wife, colleagues, former students and friends. It was so damp and cold that some kept their coats on. And he did something odd. Because he believed the moment would matter one day, he had it filmed.

He told them their competitors were “not in China, but in Silicon Valley”, and that he wanted to chase the small firms that nobody else cared about. It had to be pocket money, he said, not borrowed from family, because they would probably fail. They put what they had on the table and reached about ==500,000 yuan, or $60,000==.
Don't worry, I think the Internet dream will not die.
blocks.who: Jack Ma, filmed at the founding meeting, February 1999

blocks.text: He was 34. He had failed his way through school, been refused by employers he could name, and lost control of his first internet company. He had also spent 20 years talking to strangers, teaching rooms full of people and getting a team to follow him twice. Everything he needed for what came next, he had already practised. The company they started that day was called Alibaba.

items.text: Enters Hangzhou Teachers College on his third exam attempt.
First trip abroad, to the Morleys in Newcastle, Australia.
Graduates and starts teaching at the Hangzhou Institute of Electronic Engineering.
Founds the Hope translation agency, and keeps it alive by selling small goods.
First US trip. Malibu by his account, then Seattle and the word “beer”.
Starts China Pages with Cathy and He Yibing.
Merges with Hangzhou Telecom, loses control and leaves for a ministry job in Beijing.
Eighteen people meet in his Hangzhou flat to start Alibaba.

blocks.title: Your first two companies are your tuition
blocks.text: Hope taught Ma to keep a business alive with his own hands. China Pages taught him what giving up control feels like, and the ministry job taught him who he did and did not want to serve. He made real mistakes, above all merging with a far larger partner and losing his say. But he kept his team and his lessons, and started again with both.

factCheck.method: Built first from Jack Ma's own words: Inc. (2008), Worth (2008), the World Economic Forum conversation at Davos (2015) and his 2017 remarks in Newcastle. Duncan Clark's biography (via the licensed excerpts in Bangalore Mirror and The National) supplied the structure, cross-checked against Bloomberg, AP, the University of Hong Kong citation, the University of Newcastle and Australian press. Teaching years come from named colleagues and students quoted by Zhejiang Online, China News Service and Dushi Kuaibao. Chinese-language quotes are our own translations and are marked as such. Facts cited to the Clark book page (source 2) were read from chapters 3–4 of the text; these should be checked against a licensed copy, because the publisher page does not show them. The Davos transcript (source 5) was checked against the official session listed on Commons (source 4) only by session identity, not line by line against the audio. Source 21 is a reproduction of a magazine article inside an exam paper, so its details (the two-hour English teacher, the six colleges, the army and police school) are single-sourced and attributed to “one profile”. Source 16 is a first-person text edited from a biography, not Ma's verified words, so it is never quoted and is attributed to an account. Ma's Malibu and Las Vegas story is presented as his own account, not as established fact.

disputed.note: Bloomberg (details confirmed by company spokesmen) and AP describe his parents as pingtan performers. Clark, the NYT review and Worth give day jobs (factory worker and photographer) with pingtan or a drama association as a passion or side role. We state both.

disputed.claim: Which year he met the Morleys and how old he was
disputed.note: Ma told Inc. and Worth 1979. Clark, the University of Newcastle, the Newcastle Herald and HKU say 1980, and Clark gives July 1980. The AFR's 2016 story says he was 12, and its 2017 story says 15. We use July 1980, aged 15.

disputed.claim: When he started at the hotel, and for how long
disputed.note: Ma says he was 12 in Inc. and Worth, but 13 elsewhere, and 8 years in Inc. but 9 at Davos. Clark's visitor figures (728 foreigners in 1978, over 40,000 in 1979) suggest the routine could only have become regular at about 14 to 15. A biography-based account (source 16) says his father took him to the lake from age 8. We give the range and do not fix a start date.

disputed.claim: Where he bought Lu Yao's novel, and when the hotel turned him down
disputed.note: Ma's own words reported by Jiemian say Yiwu railway station; other Chinese accounts say Jinhua or Hangzhou station, or that he found it while delivering books. We use Yiwu. Sources also differ on whether the hotel waiter rejection followed his first exam (People's Daily Online) or his second (China Daily).

disputed.claim: When the translation agency started and what its rent was
disputed.note: Clark and Sina Finance say January or early 1994. Liu Ren, after interviewing Ma in 2002, says 1992, and other reports say the idea began taking shape in 1992. First-month rent is given as 2,000 yuan (People.cn, IT Times) or 2,400 yuan (Liu Ren). All agree revenue was 700 yuan. We use January 1994 and 2,000.

disputed.claim: Who gave him the name Jack
disputed.note: Ma at Davos and Clark say an American tourist and pen friend whose father and husband were named Jack. Some reports credit 'a foreigner' or a pen pal generally. We use Ma's own account.

disputed.claim: Maths score on the third gaokao
disputed.note: Clark, People's Daily Online (Chinese) and Chinese press say 89 out of 120. People's Daily Online (English), CPPCC Daily and Sina Education say 79. The zh-language Wikipedia gives the first score as 9, not 1. We use 89 and note 79; for the first score, 1 is reported by Clark, China Daily and People's Daily.

Most Chinese accounts say he was upgraded to a degree place because the English intake was unfilled. Clark adds that the spare places were for male students. All agree he was about five points short of the degree line.
Ma says at Davos he 'failed three times' for university; Inc. and most others say he failed twice and passed on the third attempt. We use failed twice, passed third time.

Clark places the story after the second exam, around 1983, and many retellings place it after 1988. KFC's first China store opened in Beijing in 1987 and its first Zhejiang store opened in Hangzhou in 1993, per Yum China and a KFC event report, so a teenage rejection is not possible. Ma told Inc. he was turned down for 'secretary to the general manager' around 1992, while at Davos he described 24 applicants and 23 hired. The job, count and exact date remain unverified beyond his own word.

disputed.claim: Rejections by Harvard (10) and from 30 jobs
disputed.note: These are Ma's own repeated claims, for example at Davos 2015. Harvard has not confirmed them that we could find. We report them as what he says.
Inc. and Worth say 31 days. In Newcastle in 2017 he said 29 days. We use 29, his latest and on-site statement.

Pandaily reports about A$200 over two years during college. Clark quotes Ken Morley as sending five to ten dollars a week in six-monthly cheques, which would total much more than A$200 over two years. The A$22,000 for the first home is from Clark and repeated in Indiatimes. Treat A$200 as one report.
Inc. says 100–120 yuan ($12–$15), HKU says about $14, Bloomberg says $15, and Dushi Kuaibao says 90 rising to 120 yuan. We use 90 rising to 120, about $12 to $15.

disputed.claim: Malibu, the gun, Las Vegas and the $600
disputed.note: This rests on Ma's own telling, in versions that differ, including whether a gun was flashed, whether he was held for two days or several, and how he left. Clark notes a less colourful version in the Hangzhou Daily in 1995. Ma has never named the American, and some Chinese press has named a person; we do not, as we could not verify it. Presented as his account.

disputed.claim: Emails after the first Hope web page
disputed.note: Accounts differ: The Paper and The Beijing News say five, a 2007 Sina Finance retelling says six, and People.cn says four in three hours. Ma told Inc. the search was on Yahoo, while Liu Ren says Lycos. We say five in most accounts.

IT Times and People.cn say 20,000 yuan. Inc. says $2,000 borrowed, and AP says $2,400 from relatives. A further book version gives 100,000 yuan including office assets. We use about 20,000 yuan and mention his $2,000.

Reports range from immediately after his return in March 1995 to June 1995, and one quoted remark from Ma mentions raising it in 1994. We say he left in 1995. Sources also differ on 6, 6.5 and 7 years of teaching, and Inc. and Bloomberg say five.
The Beijing News quotes 500 yuan a month and IT Times 800 yuan. We say 'almost no pay' and give neither.

Most sources say 18 people including Ma; AP says Ma and 17 friends, and HKU says Ma and 17 co-founders. Bloomberg names Joe Tsai among the 18 founders, but Tsai told Forbes he first met Ma in May 1999, so he was not in the room in February. We say 18 people gathered.
